name: Kneecap Dislocation (Patellar Instability)
seo_title: Dislocated Kneecap Treatment Palm Beach Gardens | ELITE
seo_desc: Kneecap dislocation care in Palm Beach Gardens and Port St. Lucie, from bracing and rehab to stabilization surgery, with board-certified Dr. Matarazzo.
lede: When your kneecap slides out of its groove, the knee can buckle, swell and look misshapen. First episodes are often treated without surgery, while repeat dislocations may need stabilization.
what_it_is: Your kneecap, or patella, links the thigh muscles to the shinbone and rides in a V-shaped groove at the end of the thighbone. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) explains that ligaments, muscles and the shape of the bones all work together to keep it on track. The medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL), on the inner side, keeps the kneecap from moving too far sideways and can be damaged when the kneecap dislocates toward the outside.

A dislocation means the kneecap comes fully out of its groove. A subluxation is a partial slip that pops back on its own. Patellar instability is the term for a kneecap that keeps doing either. According to the AAOS, first dislocations usually happen with a pivot, twist or awkward fall, or a direct blow. Some people are more prone because of a shallow groove, knock-kneed alignment or the way the leg bones are rotated.
symptoms: The kneecap visibly out of place or the knee looking misshapen
A pop or snap at the moment of injury
Being unable to straighten the knee or stand on it
A nervous feeling that the kneecap is about to slip out
A kneecap that moves side to side too easily
causes: A pivot, twist or awkward fall with the foot planted
A direct blow to the kneecap
A shallow or flat groove at the end of the thighbone
Knock-kneed alignment or unusual rotation of the leg bones
A patellar tendon that attaches farther to the outside than usual
A previous dislocation that stretched or tore the MPFL

how_therapy_helps.intro: The AAOS reports a relatively low recurrence rate after a first-time dislocation treated without surgery, so most people start with bracing and rehabilitation. MedlinePlus describes wearing a brace for about 3 weeks, followed by physical therapy to rebuild strength and motion. Surgery is usually reserved for repeat dislocations or for loose bone or cartilage fragments inside the joint. Dr. Matarazzo looks at the number of episodes, your anatomy on imaging and any cartilage damage before suggesting a stabilization procedure.
methods: If the kneecap stays out, it is guided back into place, often with pain medicine, and X-rays check for fractures or loose fragments.
A brace protects the healing ligament for the first few weeks before motion is gradually restored.

Strengthening the thigh and hip muscles and retraining movement helps the kneecap track. The AAOS highlights stationary cycling as a useful exercise, with a gradual return to activity over 1 to 3 months.
Some people use a patellar stabilizing brace when they return to activity to reduce the sense of instability.

For recurrent instability, surgery may reinforce the soft tissue restraints, often by reconstructing the MPFL, realign the bone, or reshape the groove. The AAOS reports a redislocation rate of less than 10% after surgery.

first_visit: Dr. Matarazzo will ask whether this was a first dislocation or a repeat episode and how it happened. He watches you walk, checks range of motion, tests how far the kneecap moves and whether pushing it outward causes apprehension, and measures limb alignment. X-rays are standard. An MRI looks for torn ligaments and bone or cartilage fragments, and a CT scan may be ordered to study alignment and the shape of the groove.
recovery: The NHS notes that many people can start walking again soon after treatment, but full recovery can take several months. For first-time dislocations treated without surgery, the AAOS describes a gradual return to activity over about 1 to 3 months after bracing and therapy. Recovery after stabilization surgery is longer and depends on which procedure is performed. MedlinePlus cautions that repeat dislocations can damage the knee further and raise the risk of arthritis, so finishing the full rehab program is worth the effort.
self_care: Keep the knee still and supported until it has been examined.
Ice the knee and keep it raised to control swelling.
Use over-the-counter pain relief if it is safe for you.
Avoid twisting and sports until strength has returned and you have been cleared.
see_a_doctor: The knee has changed shape or the kneecap is visibly out of place (go to the emergency room)
The knee becomes very swollen very quickly after an injury (go to the emergency room)
You cannot stand up or move the knee
Swelling and pain come back after the knee had been improving

faqs.q: Should I put my dislocated kneecap back in myself?
faqs.a: No. The NHS advises against trying to put the kneecap back into place yourself. A dislocated kneecap often moves back on its own, and when it does not, a clinician usually repositions it after giving strong pain relief. X-rays are typically needed afterward to look for a fracture or loose fragments, even if the kneecap has already slipped back in.

It might, but the odds are better than many people expect after a first episode. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports a relatively low recurrence rate after a first-time dislocation treated without surgery. The risk is higher for people with a shallow groove, knock-kneed alignment or earlier episodes. After stabilization surgery, the AAOS reports a redislocation rate below 10%.

faqs.q: Do you need surgery after a first kneecap dislocation?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most first-time dislocations are treated with a brace and physical therapy. Surgery may be recommended sooner when imaging shows a loose piece of bone or cartilage in the joint, or when the knee anatomy makes repeat dislocation likely. Repeat dislocations are the most common reason to consider stabilization, according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a kneecap dislocation and subluxation?
faqs.a: A dislocation means the kneecap comes completely out of its groove and may stay out until it is moved back. A subluxation is a partial slip, where the kneecap shifts toward the edge of the groove and returns on its own. Both can stretch or tear the stabilizing tissues, and repeated subluxations are treated as a form of patellar instability.

The medial patellofemoral ligament runs from the inner side of the kneecap to the thighbone and helps keep the kneecap from sliding outward. It is commonly torn during a dislocation. MPFL reconstruction replaces it with a tendon graft to restore that restraint. It is one of the soft tissue procedures the AAOS describes for recurrent instability, sometimes combined with bone realignment.

faqs.q: Can a dislocated kneecap cause arthritis?
faqs.a: It can increase the risk. MedlinePlus notes that repeat dislocations can make the condition worse and raise the chance of osteoarthritis. When the kneecap slips out, it can scrape or chip the cartilage on the back of the kneecap or the thighbone. Preventing further episodes through rehab, bracing or surgery when needed is part of protecting the joint long term.
